239 - The Philosophy of Werner Herzog: Werner Herzog is the German filmmaker behind Aguirre the Wrath of God, Fitzcarraldo, and Grizzly Man, famous for hauling a real steamship over a mountain and for documentaries that court danger in pursuit of what he calls ecstatic truth. Though he brands himself an anti-intellectual, his films stage hard questions: is nature murderous indifference, does fabrication reveal deeper truth than facts, and why does his doomed masculinity keep pursuing the useless? This book reads Herzog alongside Wittgenstein, Nietzsche, Heidegger, and Schopenhauer.
240 - Neil Young and Philosophy: Neil Young is the Canadian singer-songwriter who has made rock music since the 1960s, first with Buffalo Springfield, then with Crazy Horse and solo, known for ragged guitar epics and a stubborn refusal to repeat himself. His quirks invite philosophy: keeping flawed first takes as an ideal of authenticity, claiming songs simply arrive rather than being composed, being sued for making uncharacteristic music, and writing an album of synthesizer voices for his disabled son. Questions of authenticity, creativity, extended mind, and environmental ethics run through his career.
241 - The Philosophy of Documentary Film: Documentary film is cinema that claims to show reality rather than invent it, from Nanook of the North and Triumph of the Will to Grizzly Man and Roger and Me. That claim is exactly what makes it philosophically fertile: how can staged or edited images tell the truth, what separates a factual trace from fiction, and is it ethical to film a real death? This book brings Plato, Cavell, Bazin, and contemporary film theorists to bear on the genre's oldest promise and its darkest problems.
242 - Joss Whedon as Philosopher: Joss Whedon created the television series Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Angel, Firefly, and Dollhouse, and directed The Avengers, earning a devoted following for witty dialogue and morally serious genre stories. This book asks whether a TV writer can actually do philosophy, and answers by reading his characters through serious theory: Angel's cursed soul as a test case for personal identity, Dr. Horrible through existentialism, and The Cabin in the Woods as a clash of utilitarianism and the ethics of care.
243 - The Philosophy of Christopher Nola: Christopher Nolan is the director of Memento, The Dark Knight, Inception, and Interstellar, blockbusters famous for puzzles about memory, dreams, and time. His films are practically philosophy thought experiments in disguise: a man who cannot form memories and tattoos clues onto his body, a spinning top that may or may not confirm reality, a vigilante who wiretaps an entire city, and a father choosing between his family and the survival of the species. This book reads them through Descartes, Kant, Hobbes, and Hegel.
244 - The Who and Philosophy: Doctor Who is the long-running British science-fiction series about the Doctor, a time-traveling alien who regenerates into a new body instead of dying, protected by the TARDIS and stalked by Daleks and Cybermen. Regeneration alone is a philosopher's playground: which theory of personal identity can explain how the First and Thirteenth Doctor are the same person? The show also raises questions about time travel paradoxes, whether Daleks could be people, and what makes someone special enough to save the universe.
247 - The Ultimate Supernatural and Phil: Supernatural is the American TV series that ran from 2005 to 2020, following brothers Sam and Dean Winchester as they hunt demons, angels, and monsters across America in a black Chevy Impala. Over fifteen seasons it grew from monster-of-the-week horror into a cosmic story where the brothers literally revolt against God himself, their own author. That arc makes it rich philosophical territory: free will versus a written plan, whether immortality would be worth it, how to kill an idea, and what we owe each other.
251 - Punk Rock and Philosophy - Researc: Punk rock is the raw, confrontational music born in the mid-1970s with the Sex Pistols and the Clash, carried on by hardcore bands like Bad Religion, Refused, and NOFX, and defined by do-it-yourself ethics and distrust of authority. This book argues punk is not just a style or subculture but a philosophy of deviance: a Gramsci-inflected revolt against the mainstream that co-opts and commodifies dissent. Album by album, it asks whether rebellion can survive being sold, and what punks owe the truth.
252 - Better Call Saul and Philosophy -: Better Call Saul is the acclaimed television prequel to Breaking Bad, tracing the moral decay of lawyer Jimmy McGill as he melts into the shady criminal attorney Saul Goodman. Its slow, deliberate portrait of a good-ish man choosing badly makes it ideal philosophy material: can it be right to defend the guilty, is scamming for fun worse than scheming for profit, does a prequel rob its hero of free will, and is morality really for suckers? Kant, Hume, Hobbes, and virtue ethics all get their day in court.
253 - Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy: Isaac Asimov's Foundation is the landmark science-fiction series, begun in the 1940s, about a galactic empire doomed to collapse and the mathematician Hari Seldon, whose science of psychohistory can predict the fall of civilizations and shorten the dark age that follows. The premise opens deep questions: if history is predictable, is human freedom an illusion, can statistics about billions justify manipulating individuals, and are noble lies ever permissible? This book tests Seldon's science against Plato, Hume, chaos theory, and modern data-driven history.
